title: Farmworker Justice Fund, Inc. v. Brock; Farmworkers Justice Fund, Inc. v. Brock
citation: 811 F.2d 613, vacated as moot, 817 F.2d 890 (D.C. Cir. 1987)
lead: After years of field-sanitation rulemaking, the Secretary delayed federal action to await the states; a divided merits ruling compelled action but was vacated when a rule issued before the mandate.

actors.name: Secretary Brock and OSHA
actors.role: Labor officials postponing a federal standard

actors.name: States
actors.role: Governments whose potential regulation supported the postponement

proceedings: February 6, 1987 panel ordered a rule within thirty days of mandate; Williams dissented on merits and remedy.
May 7 panel vacated the entire February judgment and opinions as moot and terminated the case.
limits: The merits opinion, concurrence, and partial dissent all were vacated. Older litigation supplies background only. The assigned fragment omits earlier editorial pages, but complete actual 1987 decisions support this account.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A sanitation petition enters years of rulemaking
paragraphs: In September 1972 El Congreso asked the Labor Secretary to require drinking water, handwashing facilities, and toilets in agricultural fields. A December 1973 suit challenged inaction. An advisory committee approved a standard in December 1974, and a district court ordered further action in 1975. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration, or OSHA, proposed a rule in April 1976 recognizing sanitation hazards but did not finalize it.

Earlier appellate rulings respected priority-setting while requiring a timetable and rejecting indefinite abandonment of an initiated standard. A 1982 settlement required a good-faith effort to finish within thirty-one months, with explained, court-approved delay afterward. OSHA reopened the inquiry in 1983 and proposed a revised rule in March 1984 for farms with at least eleven hand-labor workers. Appropriations restrictions barred spending on farms with ten or fewer employees and no temporary labor camp.

sections.title: Brock recognizes a need but waits for state action
sections.cue: The advocates challenge a conditional two-year delay
paragraphs: After an extension to April 1985, the Secretary declined a federal rule on priorities and federalism grounds. On October 21 Secretary Brock reversed course, recognizing unacceptable health risks and a need for further regulation, but gave states eighteen months to provide adequate protection. If that failed, OSHA would issue a standard within another six months. Advocates challenged that postponement.

Chief Judge Wald and Senior District Judge Will read October as settling the need for regulation despite competing priorities, leaving only delay for state action. Judge Williams instead regarded the commitment as conditional and resource allocation as unresolved. All three nevertheless agreed the decision was reviewable rather than automatically protected by Heckler v. Chaney’s treatment of many nonenforcement choices.

sections.title: The majority separates forbidden policy grounds from permissible state protection
sections.cue: The original record does not support the projected coverage
paragraphs: Wald distinguished reviewing statutory limits from second-guessing discretion within them. Courts could determine whether Congress permitted the agency’s stated grounds even when those grounds were rational as policy. This completed rulemaking and conditional promise supplied a particular reviewable setting; the opinion did not announce a rule for every proposed-rule withdrawal.

The Occupational Safety and Health Act had already assigned federal leadership and provided § 18 approved state plans at least as effective as federal standards. A general preference for different federal-state roles could not justify withholding needed protection. Nor could the small-farm restriction justify gambling with covered workers to encourage broader state regulation. October measured state adequacy against the proposed large-farm standard, not required coverage of excluded small farms. The majority assumed the legally narrower view that federal large-farm regulation would not preempt state small-farm protection, yet still rejected the rationale.

Actual or genuinely imminent equivalent state protection could affect need, under the Chevron analysis then applied. A short delay might be justified by reasonable expectation that virtually all covered workers soon would be protected. But about 25% remained unprotected; thirty-seven states lacked standards, only two were developing them, and five new standards over preceding years did not support broad imminent action. Later reports that twelve states would not act corroborated concern, but the majority relied on the original record. Percentages including excluded small-farm workers could not minimize the benefit to covered workers.

The statute’s nationwide purpose, health urgency, and explanation requirements supplied manageable standards. Without making 100% coverage absolute, the majority found the further two-year delay unsupported after more than a decade. On February 6, 1987 it used Administrative Procedure Act § 706(1) to require promulgation within thirty days after issuance of the mandate, not automatically thirty days after the opinion.

sections.title: Will adds the settlement; Williams would remand on another ground
sections.cue: Their remedies differ from immediate promulgation
paragraphs: Will fully joined and separately found breach of the settlement. It promised a standard or a final refusal subject to review. In his account, October’s reversal mooted review of April’s refusal and left neither outcome, affirmatively prolonging obligations. The majority had found settlement issues unnecessary.

Williams agreed rulemaking refusals differed from ad hoc nonenforcement but emphasized scarce-resource deference. He saw specific considerations—small-farm limits, local variation, possible broader state coverage, and freeing inspectors—rather than an impermissible abstract federalism preference. He read October as retaining an erroneous belief that a federal large-farm rule would preempt state small-farm regulation and would remand for reconsideration under correct law.

Otherwise he disputed unreasonable delay and the compulsory-rule remedy. Predicting state responses and comparing enforcement benefits required expertise; even abuse would justify reconsideration or acceleration rather than judicial commitment to a specific rule. He also rejected Will’s settlement theory: April met the extended timetable, advocates sought reconsideration, and a timing settlement did not require adoption of the draft.

sections.title: A rule issues before the mandate
sections.cue: The entire merits disposition is vacated as moot
paragraphs: The Secretary issued field-sanitation standards and notified the panel by an April 28 letter. Because the mandate had not issued, the panel’s May 7, 1987 order vacated as moot the February opinion and judgment, Will’s concurrence, and Williams’s partial concurrence and dissent. It also dismissed rehearing as moot, terminated the docket, and directed a certified order copy instead of a formal mandate.
Thus the thirty-day command never operated through an issued mandate. The earlier reasoning remains historical with its vacatur attached; the May order did not affirm either side’s merits position.
